common_name: Extra Precoce a Grano Violetto Fava Bean (Italian Violet-Seeded Broad Bean)
scientific_name: Vicia faba 'Extra Precoce a Grano Violetto'

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or earliest spring, or in autumn in mild-winter regions for an overwintered crop; this Italian strain is bred to mature notably faster than standard favas.

directions: Long grown in home gardens across Liguria and Tuscany, this heirloom takes its name from its dark violet-to-near-black seed coat and its notably early maturity compared to standard English broad beans. Sow directly into cool, fertile soil in blocks so the sturdy stems support one another, and pinch the growing tips once the lowest pods have set to slow aphid buildup. Pods can be picked young for fresh shelling, but many Italian cooks let a portion dry fully on the plant, since the violet seed coat holds its color and the beans store and cook well for soups and purees. Because it matures earlier than most fava strains, it suits gardeners with a short cool season or those looking to free the bed for a following summer crop.

common_name: The Sutton Fava Bean (Dwarf English Heirloom Broad Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or earliest spring, or in autumn in mild-winter regions; its compact habit also suits large containers and exposed, windy plots.

directions: Bred by Suttons Seeds in England in the 1920s and still carrying a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, this is the classic dwarf broad bean, reaching only about a foot to eighteen inches tall while still setting a full crop of well-filled pods holding three to five beans apiece. The short, sturdy stems rarely need staking even in exposed or windy gardens, and the compact footprint makes it a favorite for raised beds, containers, and small-space plots where standard tall favas would sprawl. Sow directly into cool soil as early as it can be worked, spacing plants closely so they lean on one another for support, and pinch the growing tips once the lowest pods have set to discourage aphids. Harvest pods young for tender fresh shelling or let some dry fully on the plant for winter storage.

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date once soil has warmed slightly; Desi is the smaller, darker, thick-coated chickpea market class grown widely across South Asia, Ethiopia, and the Middle East, distinct from the large cream-colored Kabuli type.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch or so deep into well-drained soil once hard frost danger has passed, since chickpeas of any type quickly rot in cold, waterlogged ground. Desi types form a bushier, more branching plant than Kabuli chickpeas and set smaller, angular, thick-coated seeds ranging from tan and speckled to brown or near-black, borne one or two per small pod. The thicker seed coat makes Desi chickpeas notably more drought-tolerant in the field and is traditionally removed by splitting the dried seed into chana dal, though whole seeds can also be cooked as a firmer, earthier-flavored garbanzo bean. Let the crop dry down fully in place, harvesting once most pods have turned brittle and tan, then thresh and store the seed somewhere cool and dry.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service -- Cicer arietinum germplasm resources
Washington State University Extension -- Dry Pea and Chickpea Production
ICRISAT (International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics)

common_name: Eston Green Lentil (Small Green Culinary Lentil)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring a few weeks ahead of the last frost, since young lentil plants tolerate light frost and grow best through a long cool stretch before summer heat sets in.

directions: Released by the University of Saskatchewan's Crop Development Centre and long grown across the Canadian and northern U.S. prairies, Eston is the classic small, green-seeded lentil behind most grocery-store green lentils sold in North America. The low, wiry, bushy plants need lean soil and minimal fertility, since excess nitrogen pushes foliage at the expense of pods, and they hold up well to the light frosts common during early spring establishment. The small round seeds keep a firm bite and hold their shape better than red lentils when simmered, making them well suited to soups, pilafs, and salads. Harvest the whole plant once most pods have dried and rattle, then thresh and clean before storing the seed in a cool, dry place.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Crop Development Centre
